chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Faddal, from Thal'abah ibn Maymun, from Umar ibn Abi Bakkar, from Abu Bakr al-Hadrami, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

Indeed, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) married al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad al-Kindi to Dhuba'ah bint al-Zubayr ibn Abd al-Muttalib. He married him to it so that marriages would be humble/equal, and so that they would take the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) as a role model, and so that they would know that the most noble of them before Allah is the most pious of them.

key_terms.أَكْرَمَهُمْ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ: The most noble of them before Allah.
key_terms.الْمِقْدَادَ بْنَ الْأَسْوَدِ: Al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad, a prominent companion known for his piety and modest origins.
key_terms.ضُبَاعَةَ بِنْتَ الزُّبَيْرِ: Dhuba'ah bint al-Zubayr, a noblewoman from the Quraysh, daughter of Abd al-Muttalib's son.
key_terms.لِتَتَّضِعَ الْمَنَاكِحُ: So that marriages become humble/equal (referring to kafa'ah or suitability without excessive hierarchy).

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on social status differences in marriage according to the Prophet's example?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies that while the Prophet married al-Miqdad to a Qurayshi noblewoman, the primary purpose was to demonstrate that piety (*taqwa*) supersedes lineage, thereby dismantling tribal elitism. It serves as a foundational precedent in Shia jurisprudence for understanding *kafa'ah* not as rigid social stratification, but as a flexible standard where spiritual merit is the ultimate measure of suitability.
